ABSTRACT 34 
Introduction: Hundreds of dietary supplements are currently marketed as weight loss 35 
supplements. However, the advertised health claims of effectiveness for most of these are 36 
unproven. The purpose of this review was to critically appraise and evaluate the evidence for 37 
effectiveness of cactus pear, Opuntia ficus-indica (OFI), using data from published 38 
randomized clinical trials (RCTs). 39 
Methods: We conducted electronic searches in Medline, Embase, Amed, Cinahl and The 40 
Cochrane Library. No restrictions in age, time or language were imposed. The risk of bias in 41 
included studies was assessed using the Cochrane Collaboration criteria. Two reviewers 42 
independently determined the eligibility of included studies, assessed reporting quality, and 43 
extracted data. 44 
Results: We identified seven eligible studies, out of which five were included. The studies 45 
varied in design and reporting quality. Meta-analysis revealed a non-significant difference in 46 
body weight between OFI and controls, MD: -0.83 kg; 95% CI: -2.49 to 0.83; I
2
=93%. 47 
Significant reductions in BMI, percentage body fat, systolic and diastolic blood pressures, 48 
and total cholesterol were observed. Adverse events included gastric intolerance and flu 49 
symptoms. 50 
Conclusion: The evidence from RCTs does not indicate that supplementation with OFI 51 
generates statistically significant effects on body weight. Consumption of OFI can cause 52 
significant reductions in percentage body fat, blood pressure and total cholesterol. Few 53 
clinical trials evaluating the effects of OFI have been published. They vary in design and 54 
methodology, and are characterized by inconsistent quality of reporting. Further clinical trials 55 
evaluating the effects of OFI on body composition and metabolic parameters are warranted. 56 
 57 
Keywords: cactus; opuntia; weight loss; clinical trial; systematic review; meta-analysis 58

INTRODUCTION 60 
The increased prevalence of obesity and overweight has led to the proliferation of various 61 
dietary supplements in the market, with varying claims of effectiveness. However, evidence 62 
supporting the effectiveness for most of these products is unproven, and clinicians are 63 
sometimes uncertain about the therapeutic value of using such agents [1]. One such 64 
supplement being touted as having an anti-obesity effect is the cactus pear, Opuntia ficus-65 
indica. 66 
 67 
Opuntia ficus-indica (OFI) is a domesticated cactus plant that has been an important part of 68 
agricultural economies in the arid and semiarid regions of the world [2]. The fruits of OFI are 69 
edible, and range in colour from lime green, orange, red to purple depending on the ratios or 70 
concentrations of its constituent pigments [3]. Cactus pear is rich in betalains which are 71 
bioactive compounds thought to be responsible for its positive health effects [4]. Aside from 72 
its nutritional use, the cactus pear is thought to possess antioxidant and anti-inflammatory 73 
properties [5,6,7], and has been used as an artificial sweetener in the food industry [8]. In 74 
humans, consumption of OFI has been shown to improve platelet function [9] and also confer 75 
protection against peptic ulcer [10]. 76 
 77 
More recently, there has been an increased interest into the possible role of OFI in the 78 
management of obesity and body metabolic parameters. Results of animal research have 79 
suggested that OFI intake can lead to reductions in body weight via diuresis [11], decrease 80 
blood glucose by enhancing basal plasma insulin concentration [12,13], and improve lipid 81 
profile through scavenging of intracellular radicals [14,15,16]. Randomized and non-82 
randomized human studies have shown that OFI could attenuate postprandial hyperglycemia 83 
by stimulating glucose uptake in the peripheral tissues [17,18,19]. Studies in humans have 84

also demonstrated that consumption of OFI causes marked reductions in total and low-density 85 
lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol and triglycerides in subjects with dyslipidemias by up 86 
regulating binding of LDL receptors in the liver [20,21]. 87 
 88 
Clinical trials examining the effect of OFI on body weight and composition, and lipid profile 89 
have been conducted, but the effectiveness of this supplement as a weight loss aid is not 90 
established. Therefore, the objective of this review was to critically appraise and evaluate the 91 
evidence for effectiveness of OFI as a weight loss supplement, using data from published 92 
trials in humans. 93 
 94 
METHODS 95 
Electronic searches were conducted in the following databases: Medline, Embase, Amed, 96 
Cinahl, and The Cochrane Library. Each database was searched from inception up until April, 97 
2013. The search terms used included opuntia, neopuntia, cactus, cactus pear, spineless 98 
cactus, prickly pear, nopal, litramine, body weight, overweight, obesity, weight loss, body 99 
composition, body fat, waist circumference, cholesterol, triglycerides, systolic blood 100 
pressure, diastolic blood pressure, blood sugar, and derivatives of these (a Medline search 101 
strategy has been included as appendix 1). No age, gender or language restrictions were 102 
imposed. We also searched Google Scholar for relevant conference proceedings, and hand 103 
searched the bibliography of retrieved articles. 104 
 105 
Only blinded randomized clinical trials (RCTs) were included in the review. To be 106 
considered for inclusion, studies had to test the effectiveness of orally administered OFI as a 107 
weight loss supplement in normal or overweight volunteers. Included studies had to report 108 
body weight or composition as an outcome. Studies were included irrespective of duration of 109

intervention or lifestyle adjustments incorporated into their trial regimen. Trials testing OFI 110 
as part of a combination supplement, i.e. dietary interventions containing other weight loss 111 
supplements in addition to OFI, were excluded from the review. 112 
 113 
The risk of bias for included studies was assessed using the Cochrane Collaboration risk of 114 
bias tool kit [22] which examines the following domains: sequence generation; allocation 115 
concealment; blinding of care-providers and participants; blinding of outcome assessors; 116 
incomplete outcome data; selective reporting; and other biases. Our primary outcome 117 
measures were body weight and composition. Secondary outcomes measures were systolic 118 
blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, total, LDL and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) 119 
cholesterol, triglycerides and blood glucose. We also documented data on adverse events. 120 
Two reviewers (IJO and JOS) independently determined the eligibility of studies, assessed 121 
the risk of bias of included studies, and extracted the data according to study design, 122 
participants' characteristics, interventions and results. Any disagreements were resolved 123 
through consensus. 124 
 125 
Using standard meta-analysis software (RevMan 5.2) [23], we computed mean differences 126 
(MD) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for studies with sufficient data for statistical 127 
pooling. The random-effects model was used for meta-analyses [24]. Sensitivity analyses 128 
(analysing trials based on methodology) were used to investigate heterogeneity, using the I
2 
129 
statistic; values of 25%, 50%, and 75% indicated low, medium, and high statistical 130 
heterogeneity respectively. Where reported data were inadequate for statistical pooling, the 131 
results were presented in a narrative format. 132

RESULTS 135 
Our electronic searches identified 76 non-duplicate citations, out of which seven eligible 136 
studies were identified (Figure 1). One RCT was excluded because it did not report relevant 137 
outcomes [25], and another because OFI was combined with other weight loss supplements 138 
[26]. Thus, five RCTs with a total of 382 participants were included in the review 139 
[27,28,29,30,31]. 140 
 141 
There were variations in the risk of bias across the included studies (Figure 2). Only 40% of 142 
the RCTs adequately reported methods of sequence generation, and none adequately reported 143 
how allocation was concealed. Two RCTs (40%) showed a low risk of performance bias, 144 
while 80% of the RCTs had a low risk of attrition and reporting biases. Three RCTs (60%) 145 
showed high risk of other biases, and two performed intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis. 146 
 147 
Four RCTs were of parallel design and placebo-controlled, while one was quasi-experimental 148 
in design, and had no placebos [27] (Table 1). Participants in one RCT [27] were exclusively 149 
females with hypercalciuria, those in another two were described as overweight and obese 150 
[28,29], while those in the remaining two had metabolic syndrome [30,31]. The participants’ 151 
their ages ranged from 20 to 60 years. Four RCTs incorporated lifestyle changes into their 152 
trial regimen; these included low to normal caloric intakes, high protein diet, and physical 153 
activity [27,29,30,31]. The lifestyle changes in one RCT were not specified [28]. Dietary 154 
compliance was monitored through food diaries in four RCTs [27,28,29,30]; one of these also 155 
used measurements of the amounts of empty food packages returned and weekly phone calls 156 
to participants for monitoring. One RCT did not report the method used to monitor 157 
compliance [31]. Body composition was estimated in four RCTs by dual-energy X-ray 158 
absorptiometry [27], air-displacement plethysmography [28], bio-impedance [29], and whole 159

DISCUSSION 236 
Main findings 237 
The results of our meta-analysis indicate that supplementation with OFI does not generate 238 
statistically significant reductions in body weight and waist circumference. The results also 239 
suggest that OFI ingestion results in significant reductions in BMI, percentage body fat, 240 
systolic and diastolic blood pressures, and total cholesterol. The results of the meta-analysis 241 
should be interpreted with caution because of the high heterogeneity observed in some of the 242 
analyses, and lack of consistency in the direction of study results between the overall and 243 
sensitivity analyses. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic review evaluating the 244 
effect of OFI supplementation on body weight and cardiovascular risk factors using data from 245 
published RCTs. 246 
 247 
Opuntia ficus-indica-containing products are commonly marketed over-the-counter and on 248 
the internet with trade names XLS medical and Proactol, and reported as “certified medical 249 
devices clinically proven” to generate losses in body weight and fat [32,33]. Apart from its 250 
purported diuretic actions, gastrointestinal motility studies have suggested that OFI appears to 251 
inhibit phosphodiesterase in the intestinal smooth muscles, an effect which results in a delay 252 
in gastric emptying time [34]. The results of our meta-analyses, however, fail to demonstrate 253 
that these reported mechanisms translate to significant reductions in body weight. The effect 254 
sizes for the observed reductions in percentage body fat and BMI are small, and do not reach 255 
clinical significance [35]. The significant reduction in BMI appears due largely to the 256 
influence of the largest trial which also reported significant reductions in body weight [29]. 257

Removal of this trial from the meta-analysis resulted in a non-significant difference in BMI 258 
between OFI and placebo. 259 
 260 
We observed significant reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressure with OFI. Cactus 261 
pear fruits contain variable amounts of polyphenols [36,37], and research has shown that 262 
intake of food products rich in this group of bioactive components can have positive effects 263 
on blood pressure [38,39]. The effect sizes of these reductions, though small, could be 264 
beneficial in the preventive management of hypertension. However, the trueness of this effect 265 
is debatable, and it is unclear at this point whether the reductions observed in our results can 266 
be sustained over the medium- to long-term. 267 
 268 
While a beneficial effect was seen for total cholesterol, we did not observe any evidence from 269 
our meta-analyses that supplementation with OFI generates beneficial effects on other blood 270 
lipid parameters. Results of animal studies have shown that the purported positive effects of 271 
OFI on blood lipid profile are accomplished through a variety of mechanisms which include 272 
boosting the serum concentration of adiponectin, promoting greater availability of mRNA 273 
which code for genes involved in lipid metabolism, and stimulating hepatic synthesis of 274 
carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 and microsomal TG transfer proteins [40,41]. However, the 275 
results of our review suggest that these findings are not being replicated in humans, and this 276 
is quite disappointing. In an assessment of health claims, The European Food Safety 277 
Authority (EFSA) concluded that a cause and effect relationship between the consumption of 278 
NeOpuntia® and the claimed beneficial effects on blood lipid profile and cardiovascular risk 279 
is unproven [42]. 280

Preliminary findings from a systematic review of non-randomized studies suggested that 282 
ingestion of OFI causes marked acute reductions in blood sugar levels [43]. The results of the 283 
two RCTs included in the review, however, failed to show that these reductions were 284 
significant when compared with controls, and were not also sustained over time. In a cross-285 
over study to evaluate the effectiveness of OFI in management of diabetes, the investigators 286 
observed that beneficial effects on glucose (and cholesterol) only occurred after intake of a 287 
total of 30 capsules daily. They concluded that total number of capsules required to be 288 
consumed daily to achieve this effect is impractical [44]. These findings cast major doubts on 289 
the appropriateness of the use of OFI supplements as anti-diabetic agents. 290 
 291 
Lifestyle interventions are an important component of weight management [45]. Most of the 292 
RCTs included in the review reduced caloric intake of trial participants, and also incorporated 293 
exercise therapy into their trial regimen. It is well established that a hypocaloric diet coupled 294 
with physical activity can generate significant reductions in body weight and fat [46,47]. 295 
Whether lifestyle changes blunted or enhanced the effect of OFI in this study is unclear. 296 
Furthermore, the wide variation in dosages across the included studies makes it difficult to 297 
ascertain minimum effective dose of OFI. 298 
 299 
While the adverse events reported with the use of OFI were reported as generally mild, intake 300 
of OFI supplements does not appear to be entirely risk-free. Consumption of cactus pear was 301 
suspected to have triggered hypoglycaemic episodes in diabetic patients on conventional oral 302 
hypoglycemic medication [48,49]. Immunological reactions to its ingestion have also been 303 
reported [50,51]. These reports suggest that more surveillance to monitor for suspected 304 
adverse effects is imperative. 305

Strength and limitations 307 
This is the first review evaluating the effectiveness and safety of this popular weight loss 308 
supplement. We employed a robust strategy to search for studies, and we accounted for the 309 
methodological quality of included studies. We also performed sensitivity analyses to test the 310 
robustness of overall results. However, we recognize several limitations. We may not have 311 
identified all available studies evaluating the effects of OFI on body weight and 312 
cardiovascular risk factors, especially unpublished studies. The number of included studies is 313 
few, and most are bereft of adequate sample sizes, and also vary in their design and 314 
methodology (as seen in sensitivity analyses). Furthermore, we could not perform subgroup 315 
analyses. 316 
 317 
Implications for research 318 
Larger well-controlled randomized clinical trials examining the effect of OFI on body 319 
composition and metabolic parameters are required to allow for a better assessment of its 320 
effects. These trials should be well-reported in line with standardized guidelines. Anything 321 
less will not provide important information or conclusively demonstrate a benefit of cactus 322 
pear, if one exists. Studies investigating the effects of OFI intake on blood pressure, and 323 
further evaluation of its mechanisms of action in humans should be investigated. Research 324 
into appropriate doses of OFI that could generate clinically beneficial effects in humans is 325 
also needed. 326 
 327 
Implications for practice 328 
Consumption of fruits is widely recommended for healthy lifestyles, and intake of cactus pear 329 
can form part of a well-balanced diet. The evidence from published RCTs does not show that 330 
OFI intake has beneficial effects on body weight. There is some evidence which suggests that 331

OFI generates small reductions in percentage body fat, BMI and total cholesterol; these 332 
reductions are too small to be of clinical relevance. OFI consumption could potentially lead 333 
to reductions in blood pressure, but it should not be recommended as a substitute for current 334 
hypertensive management. The intake of OFI extracts could interact with anti-diabetic 335 
medication, and diabetic patients on oral hypoglycemics should be cautious about consuming 336 
OFI-containing supplements. 337 
 338 
CONCLUSIONS 339 
The evidence from published RCTs does not show that OFI intake has beneficial effects on 340 
body weight. Evidence also suggests that OFI generates beneficial effects on percentage body 341 
fat, BMI and total cholesterol; the effect sizes are small, and the clinical relevance is 342 
doubtful. OFI appears to cause significant reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressures. 343 
Few clinical trials evaluating the effects of OFI have been published; they vary in design and 344 
methodology, and the majority are characterized by flaws in reporting quality. Further 345 
clinical trials evaluating the effects of OFI on body composition and cardiovascular profile 346 
are warranted. 347

Highlights 
• The cactus pear, Opuntia ficus-indica (OFI), is marketed under trade names such as 
Proactol and XLS medical, with “certified” claims of clinical efficacy in obesity 
management 
• Opuntia ficus-indica-containing supplements are also being marketed as antidiabetic 
agents 
• The results from our meta-analysis of published clinical trials does not indicate that 
OFI supplementation has significant beneficial effects on body weight 
• Our meta-analytic results suggest that OFI intake causes significant reductions in 
BMI, percentage body fat and total; however, the effect sizes are small and do not 
reach clinical significance 
• Few clinical trials evaluating the effects of OFI in obesity management have been 
conducted; they vary in design and methodology
